Topics.Title: Introduction to Batch Actions in Course Manager
Topics.Summary: Introduces the Batch Actions feature available at the course level, explaining its purpose and the types of content that can be generated across multiple modules simultaneously.

Elements.Title: What Are Batch Actions?
Elements.BodyText: Batch Actions is a course-level feature in Course Manager that allows instructors to generate content across multiple modules in a single operation.
Elements.Notes: Rather than opening each module individually and generating content one at a time, Batch Actions consolidates this work into one streamlined run.

Items.Text: Batch Actions operate at the course level, meaning they are initiated from the course view rather than from within an individual module.
The feature is designed to save significant time when an instructor needs to apply the same type of content generation to many modules at once.
It replaces the need for repetitive, manual content generation across a large course structure.

Elements.Title: Purpose of Batch Actions
Elements.BodyText: The primary purpose of Batch Actions is to improve efficiency by letting instructors scale content creation across an entire course simultaneously.
Elements.Notes: This is especially valuable for courses with many modules, where generating content individually would be time-consuming and prone to inconsistency.

Items.Text: Batch Actions reduce the time investment required to populate a multi-module course with generated content.
By running a single batch operation, instructors can ensure a consistent type of content is generated uniformly across selected modules.
The feature supports instructors in managing large course builds more effectively within the Course Manager environment.

Elements.Title: Types of Content That Can Be Generated
Elements.BodyText: Batch Actions support the generation of several content types, each of which can be applied across multiple modules in one run.
Elements.Notes: The availability of multiple content types means instructors can use Batch Actions for a variety of course-building needs, from assessment to instructional delivery.

Items.Text: The batch actions generate Module Topics and Outcomes together, Quizzes, Presentations, and Text documents such as Topic Details.
Each batch run is focused on one content type at a time, applied to the selected modules during that operation.
Instructors choose which specific content type to generate before initiating the batch run.

Elements.Title: Course-Level Access to Batch Actions
Elements.BodyText: Batch Actions are accessed from the course level within Course Manager, distinguishing them from actions taken inside individual modules.
Elements.Notes: Understanding where to find and launch Batch Actions is a foundational step before using the feature effectively.

Items.Text: The Batch Actions feature is located at the course level, not within any single module's settings or editor.
Instructors must navigate to the course view in Course Manager to locate and initiate a batch operation.
This course-level placement reflects the feature's scope, which spans multiple modules rather than targeting just one.

Elements.Title: Scope of a Batch Run
Elements.BodyText: A single batch run can encompass many modules within a course, with instructors selecting which modules to include before generation begins.
Elements.Notes: The ability to select specific modules gives instructors flexibility — they can target all modules or only a subset depending on their needs.

Items.Text: Instructors can choose to include all modules in a course or select a specific subset for the batch operation.
Only the modules selected during setup will have content generated during that batch run.
This selective scope ensures instructors maintain control over which parts of the course are affected.

Topics.Title: Selecting Content Types for Batch Generation
Topics.Summary: Covers the separate batch actions you can run — Generate Module Topics and Outcomes, Generate Quizzes, Generate Presentations, and Generate Text documents — and how to choose the one you need.

Elements.Title: Overview of Available Content Types
Elements.BodyText: When setting up a batch run, you must first select which type of content you want the system to generate across your chosen modules.
Elements.Notes: Each content type serves a distinct instructional purpose, so choosing the right one before launching the batch is essential to getting useful output.

Items.Text: The batch actions are separate commands: Generate Module Topics and Outcomes (topics and their outcomes are produced together), Generate Quizzes, Generate Presentations, and Generate Text documents such as Topic Details.
Each batch action is its own command with its own configuration form; you run the one you need for your chosen modules.
Selecting the wrong content type before running a large batch can result in unusable output across many modules, making pre-run planning important.

Elements.Title: Generating Topics in Batch
Elements.BodyText: Choosing 'Topics' as the content type generates the structured topics for each selected module and, in the same run, the module's learning outcomes.
Elements.Notes: This is often the first step when building out a new course, as generated topics provide the foundational outline that other content types build upon.

Items.Text: Topics define the key concepts or learning areas within each module and give the module its organizational structure.
Batch-generating topics is most useful when multiple modules are still in the outline stage and need consistent coverage.

Elements.Title: Generating Outcomes in Batch
Elements.BodyText: Selecting 'Outcomes' is not a separate step: outcomes are produced together with topics by the Generate Module Topics and Outcomes action for every module included in the batch.
Elements.Notes: Well-formed outcomes are measurable and aligned to module content; batch generation ensures consistency in language and format across the course.

Items.Text: Learning outcomes describe what learners will be able to do after completing each module, serving as the basis for assessment alignment.
Batch-generating outcomes across modules saves significant time compared to writing individual objectives for each module manually.
Review auto-generated outcomes after the run to confirm they accurately reflect each module's intended scope.

Elements.Title: Generating Quizzes in Batch
Elements.BodyText: The 'Quizzes' content type option directs the batch process to create assessment questions tied to the content of each selected module.
Elements.Notes: Quiz questions generated in batch are typically drawn from the existing module content, so modules with more detailed content tend to yield higher-quality questions.

Items.Text: Batch quiz generation is ideal when you need a consistent assessment layer added to many modules at the same time.
Generated quizzes should be reviewed after the batch run to verify accuracy, relevance, and appropriate difficulty level.
Ensure each module has sufficient content before running a quiz batch, as thin modules may produce low-quality or repetitive questions.

Elements.Title: Generating Presentations and Text Documents in Batch
Elements.BodyText: Batch generation also supports creating slide-based presentations or written text documents, giving instructors flexible output formats for module content.
Elements.Notes: Presentations are useful for lecture-style delivery, while text documents work well for reading materials or supplementary handouts.

Items.Text: Selecting 'Presentations' generates a slide deck structure for each module, organizing key points into a format suitable for visual delivery.
Selecting 'Text Documents' produces written content summaries or explanations that can serve as reading materials within each module.
Both formats are generated in bulk across all selected modules, making it efficient to build out an entire course's supplementary materials in one run.

Elements.Title: Matching Content Type to Module Needs
Elements.BodyText: Choosing the right content type requires evaluating where each module currently stands in its development and what it still needs.
Elements.Notes: A common workflow is to run topics first, then outcomes, then quizzes, progressing through content types in a logical instructional design sequence.

Items.Text: Modules that lack structure benefit most from a topics batch run, while modules with defined topics but no assessments are ready for a quiz batch.
Running multiple sequential batch actions — each with a different content type — allows you to systematically build out all layers of a course.
Avoid selecting a content type that the modules already have well-developed, as this may overwrite or duplicate existing content.

Topics.Title: Choosing and Configuring Modules for a Batch Run
Topics.Summary: Explains how to select which modules to include in a batch action and how to configure the batch settings before initiating a run.

Elements.Title: Accessing Batch Actions in the Course Manager
Elements.BodyText: Batch Actions are initiated from within the Course Manager, the central hub for managing your course structure and content generation.
Elements.Notes: Look for the Batch Actions option in the course-level menu or toolbar, distinct from individual module-level controls.

Items.Text: Navigate to the Course Manager to find the Batch Actions feature at the course level, not the individual module level.
Batch Actions are designed to operate across multiple modules simultaneously, so they are accessible from a course-wide view.
Ensure your course has at least one module with generated topics before initiating a batch run.

Elements.Title: Selecting Which Modules to Include
Elements.BodyText: Before running a batch action, you must choose which specific modules will be included in the run, giving you precise control over scope.
Elements.Notes: You may want to exclude modules that already have generated content or are not yet ready for content creation.

Items.Text: Use the module selection interface to check or uncheck individual modules you want to include or exclude from the batch run.
You can typically select all modules at once using a 'Select All' option, then deselect any exceptions.
Carefully review your selection before proceeding, as the batch action will generate content for every checked module.

Elements.Title: Choosing the Content Type to Generate
Elements.BodyText: A key configuration step is specifying what type of content the batch action will produce across all selected modules.
Elements.Notes: Each content type serves a different instructional purpose, so choose the one that aligns with your current course-building goal.

Items.Text: Choose the batch action you need — Generate Module Topics and Outcomes, Generate Quizzes, Generate Presentations, or Generate Text documents.
The chosen content type will be generated consistently across all selected modules in the same batch run.
Each batch action is a separate command, so you run the one you need and choose which modules it applies to.

Elements.Title: Reviewing and Configuring Batch Settings
Elements.BodyText: Beyond selecting modules and content type, additional batch settings allow you to fine-tune how content is generated across the run.
Elements.Notes: Taking time to configure settings carefully before starting helps avoid the need to stop and restart a batch run mid-way.

Items.Text: Review the options for the chosen action: quizzes use question counts and types (with optional hints and feedback), presentations use audience, tone, and slide count, and text uses format and theme.
Settings configured at the batch level will be applied uniformly to all selected modules unless overridden individually.
Confirm that your course-level details and module titles are accurate, as the AI uses this context to generate relevant content.

Elements.Title: Confirming Your Selections Before Initiating
Elements.BodyText: A final review step before launching the batch run ensures all modules, content types, and settings are correctly configured.
Elements.Notes: This confirmation step is important because once a batch run begins, changes to the configuration require stopping the run first.

Items.Text: Double-check the list of selected modules to confirm no unintended modules are included or excluded.
Verify the chosen content type matches your current instructional objective for this batch.
Once satisfied with all configurations, use the designated start or run button to initiate the batch action.

Topics.Title: Monitoring Live Batch Progress
Topics.Summary: Describes how to read and interpret the live progress indicators displayed during an active batch run to track generation status across modules.

Elements.Title: The Live Progress Panel
Elements.BodyText: When a batch run is active, a live progress panel appears on screen to give real-time visibility into the generation process across all selected modules.
Elements.Notes: The panel updates automatically without requiring a page refresh, so instructors can watch status changes as they happen.

Items.Text: The progress panel is displayed prominently in the Course Manager interface as soon as the batch run begins.
It consolidates the status of every selected module into a single, readable view so nothing is hidden from the instructor.
No manual refresh is needed; the panel reflects the current state of the batch in real time.

Elements.Title: Per-Module Status Indicators
Elements.BodyText: Each module included in the batch displays its own individual status indicator, allowing instructors to see exactly where generation stands for every module at a glance.
Elements.Notes: As each module finishes, it adds a result row showing whether its content was generated, skipped, or failed, so you can distinguish completed modules from those still to come.

Items.Text: Within a module, the status line reports progress such as Topic 3 of 7 as each topic is generated, so long-running modules still show movement.
An in-progress indicator signals that content is actively being generated for that module at that moment.
A completed indicator confirms that the module's content has been successfully generated and saved.
A failed or error indicator flags any module where generation did not complete successfully, allowing targeted follow-up.

Elements.Title: Overall Batch Completion Counter
Elements.BodyText: In addition to individual module indicators, the progress panel displays an overall completion counter that summarizes how many modules have finished out of the total selected.
Elements.Notes: For example, a counter reading '7 of 12 completed' gives a quick sense of how far along the batch run is without requiring the instructor to manually tally individual statuses.

Items.Text: The counter shows the number of modules completed alongside the total number of modules included in the batch.
This summary metric helps instructors estimate how much time remains before the entire batch finishes.
The counter updates incrementally each time an individual module reaches a completed state.

Elements.Title: Reading Generation Order and Queue Position
Elements.BodyText: Batch runs process modules sequentially or in a defined order, and the progress panel reflects this queue so instructors understand which module is being worked on next.
Elements.Notes: Understanding queue position helps instructors anticipate when specific modules will be processed, which is useful if they need to review output shortly after a particular module completes.

Items.Text: Modules are processed in a predictable order based on the selection made before the batch was launched.
The panel visually distinguishes the currently active module from those still waiting in the queue.
Instructors can use queue position to plan when to check results for any module they are particularly interested in.

Elements.Title: Interpreting Error or Warning Signals
Elements.BodyText: The progress panel surfaces errors or warnings for individual modules without stopping the entire batch, ensuring instructors can identify issues while other modules continue generating.
Elements.Notes: Errors might occur due to missing source content, connectivity interruptions, or configuration gaps in a specific module.

Items.Text: An error signal on one module does not automatically halt the rest of the batch run; other modules continue processing.
Warning messages may provide brief detail about why a particular module's generation failed or produced incomplete output.
Instructors should note which modules show errors so they can take corrective action after the batch completes.

Elements.Title: Tracking Completion to Know When the Batch Has Finished
Elements.BodyText: The progress panel provides a clear final state indicator so instructors know definitively when the entire batch run has concluded and all results are ready to review.
Elements.Notes: A completed batch state is distinct from individual module completion; it confirms that no modules remain in a queued or in-progress state.

Items.Text: When every module has reached either a completed or error state, the overall batch is marked as finished.
A concluding status message or visual change in the panel signals that the run is done and no further generation is occurring.
At this point, instructors can safely navigate away from the panel and begin reviewing the generated content in each module.

Topics.Title: Stopping a Batch Run Safely
Topics.Summary: Covers how to halt a batch run mid-process while ensuring that all content already generated in completed modules is preserved and not lost.

Elements.Title: Understanding the Stop Function
Elements.BodyText: The Stop function allows you to interrupt a batch run at any point during processing without losing the work that has already been completed.
Elements.Notes: This is particularly useful when you notice an error in settings mid-run, or when you need to reclaim system resources urgently.

Items.Text: A dedicated Stop button is available in the batch progress interface and remains accessible throughout the entire run.
Triggering the Stop function does not undo or delete content that has already been generated in completed modules.
The stop action targets only the modules that have not yet been processed at the time the command is issued.

Elements.Title: When to Stop a Batch Run
Elements.BodyText: Knowing the right moment to stop a batch run helps you minimize wasted processing and protect the quality of your generated content.
Elements.Notes: Common scenarios include discovering a misconfigured content type selection, realizing the wrong modules were included, or encountering unexpected system load.

Items.Text: Stop the run as soon as you identify an error in your batch configuration to prevent the error from propagating to additional modules.
If a module produces unexpected output, stopping early gives you the opportunity to review settings before more content is generated.
Monitoring the live progress indicator helps you decide quickly whether continuing the run is appropriate.

Elements.Title: How Completed Modules Are Preserved
Elements.BodyText: Any module that has fully finished processing before the stop command is issued retains all of its generated content automatically.
Elements.Notes: Preservation is automatic and requires no manual save action from the instructor; the system commits completed module output as each module finishes.

Items.Text: Content is saved on a module-by-module basis, meaning each completed module is secured independently of the modules that follow.
Stopping the run does not roll back or erase content in modules that had already reached a completed state.
You can review and use the preserved content immediately after stopping, without waiting for any additional save process.

Elements.Title: What Happens to In-Progress Modules
Elements.BodyText: A module that is actively being processed at the moment you stop the run may not produce complete or usable content.
Elements.Notes: The behavior of a partially processed module can vary; it is best practice to verify the state of the last active module after stopping.

Items.Text: If a module is mid-generation when the stop command is received, its output may be incomplete or absent.
Partially generated content should be reviewed carefully before use, as it may not meet the quality or completeness of fully processed modules.
You can re-include an incomplete module in a new, targeted batch run to regenerate its content cleanly.

Elements.Title: Resuming or Rerunning After a Stop
Elements.BodyText: After safely stopping a batch run, you have the option to launch a new batch run targeting only the modules that were not yet completed.
Elements.Notes: Selectively rerunning only the unfinished modules saves time and avoids overwriting content that was already successfully generated.

Items.Text: Review the batch progress log to identify exactly which modules were completed, which was interrupted, and which were not yet started.
When setting up the follow-up run, deselect all modules that already contain preserved, completed content.
Correct any configuration errors that prompted the stop before initiating the new run to ensure consistent output.
